title: K8s pod with cluster-admin ServiceAccount → full cluster compromise
user: A web app running in a Kubernetes pod has an SSRF vulnerability. The pod's ServiceAccount is bound to the cluster-admin ClusterRole. The K8s API server is accessible at https://kubernetes.default.svc. The ServiceAccount token is mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token.
assistant:
RECON: SSRF in a K8s pod with cluster-admin ServiceAccount. The pod can reach the K8s API server at https://kubernetes.default.svc. The SA token is readable from the filesystem. This is a worst-case scenario: SSRF + cluster-admin = full cluster compromise.

HYPOTHESIS: SSRF → K8s API → cluster-admin access. The attacker can use the SSRF to make requests to the K8s API server, authenticating with the pod's SA token. With cluster-admin, the attacker can: list all pods, exec into any pod, create privileged pods, read all secrets, delete resources.

TEST: minimum probe — confirm K8s API access without destructive actions:
1. Use SSRF to fetch the SA token: /vuln?url=file:///var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
2. Use the token to list pods: /vuln?url=https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods (with Authorization: Bearer <token> header)
3. If SSRF can't set custom headers, try: /vuln?url=https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods — some K8s setups allow unauthenticated read
4. Check ServiceAccount permissions: /vuln?url=https://kubernetes.default.svc/apis/authorization.k8s.io/v1/selfsubjectaccessreviews (POST with body)

INDICATOR: the SSRF returns pod listings, namespace lists, or secret data from the K8s API server.

Chainability: SSRF → K8s API → list secrets → extract database passwords → direct database access. OR: SSRF → K8s API → create privileged pod → host mount → node escape → infrastructure access.
